rel.basis: Allen says De ente takes the Aristotelian side, presents a basically Thomist position, and dismisses the Parmenides and Sophist as dialectical games; Sudduth says Pico sets out to reconcile the Aristotelian identity of one and being with the Platonist priority of the one, i.e. to find both sides right rather than to take one.

Howlett summarises De ente as arguing that God is both the One and Being and that Plato and Aristotle agree; Sudduth says Pico reconciles the Aristotelian identity of the One and Being with the Platonist priority of the One.
Edelheit says Pico wished to show concord between Plato and Aristotle on unum and ens; Sudduth states the same reconciling aim.
Miller says the treatise was written to show a merely verbal disagreement between Plato and Aristotle on the one and being, which is the reconciliation Sudduth describes.

warrants.t: The essay cites Pico's own words on God as the plenitude of existence (note 20, On Being and the One, p. 44).

rel.basis: Sudduth reports that Pico distinguishes two senses of being and that Aristotle used being in the first sense, restating Pico's own distinction in the treatise between being as all that is outside nothing and being as what participates existence.

Sudduth's report that the second sense of being makes Aristotle's view compatible with the Platonist one restates Pico's own claim that the second sense permits saying something may be placed above being.

judged.justification: Concise statement of how the concord works: two senses of 'being', so that the Aristotelian identity does not put the One under Being.

quotes.t: Pico’s view here reproduces the Thomistic position that God is ipsum esse, the act of existence of itself.

warrants.t: Sudduth's note 21 points to the Summa theologiae of Aquinas (Ia, q. 4, a. 2, corp.).

rel.basis: Sudduth reads Pico's God as ipsum esse, reproducing the Thomistic position; Miller says Pico's metaphysic of existence derives from Thomas.

Miller explains that Aquinas based metaphysics on the real distinction between what participates existence and the act of existing itself, the Thomistic ground of the position Sudduth attributes to Pico.

quotes.t: Pico distinguished between the ultramundane, celestial, and sublunary worlds. The last world is the one inhabited by all living things on earth. The first is the angelic realm (as described by theologians) or the intelligible realm (as described by Platonists). …

quotes.t: Pico is explicit that the basis for his method of allegorical interpretation is a metaphysical principle of the mutual containment of all levels of reality
It is because all things are contained in each other that discourse about any one level of reality is bound to involve reference to other levels of reality.

warrants.t: The essay quotes Pico's Heptaplus for the exchange of natures and names among the worlds.
warrants.q: Bound by chains of concord, all these worlds exchange natures as well as names with mutual liberality.

judged.justification: Ties the doctrine of the worlds (and so of the angelic world) to hermeneutic method.

rel.basis: Still quotes the same Heptaplus passage and says Pico is less definite about what the higher intellect is, God or a mind akin to man's.

Still says Pico is undecided whether the higher intellect is God or a mind akin to man; Black adds that although Pico does not refute the view that it is God, his sympathies seem to lie with the view that it is nearer to and cognate with man.

Still says Pico stops short of identifying the higher intellect with the agent intellect; Howlett offers, as a gloss of her own and with a hedge, that it might be called the divine active intellect, the Spirit of the Lord or the Kabbalistic Metatron.

judged.justification: Records that Pico leaves the identity of the illuminating intellect open.

rel.basis: Black reports that the Conclusiones take up Averroes on the unicity of the intellect, the textual ground for the essay's claim that Pico apparently entertained that doctrine.

Black says none of the intellect conclusions were censured or defended in the Apologia, so where Pico himself stood cannot always be determined, which limits Still's claim about what Pico apparently entertained.

Still reports that Pico 'apparently entertained the Averroistic doctrine of the unicity of intellect ... against ... contemporary Florentine Platonists like Ficino'; Black's independent account that Pico 'did not try to arbitrate the internal disputes about the intellect' but instead 'sought to defuse them' by appeal to a higher felicity supports the picture of Pico declining to side with Ficino's Platonist intellect-doctrine.

judged.justification: Places Pico against Ficino on the unity of the intellect, a separate-substance question.

rel.basis: Both read the Oration as placing cherubic contemplation between the seraphim (love) and the thrones (justice or active life of moral virtue).

Still has contemplation of the cherubim between the thrones' active life and the seraphim's unitive love; Copenhaver translates the Oration passage in which the Cherub prepares us for Seraphic fire and lights our way toward the judgment of Thrones.
Still and Copenhaver agree that Pico arranged the highest three orders so that Thrones govern the active life, Cherubs the contemplative middle, and Seraphs the unitive love at the summit.

judged.justification: Maps the three orders onto three lives with the seraph highest.

rel.basis: Still and Copenhaver agree that Pico's Dionysian ordering has judgment (Thrones) and love (Seraphim) needing the Cherub's illuminating knowledge between them.

judged.justification: Reads the Oration's philosophical stages through Dionysian angelology.

quotes.t: This is that midday light, which, perpendicular, inflames the Seraphim, and at the same time illuminates the Cherubim.”

rel.basis: Still and Copenhaver both read the midday light passage as inflaming the Seraphim and, at the same time, illuminating the Cherubim.

rel.basis: Still notes that Pico's later De ente et uno calls even angelic intellectual knowledge imperfect; Pico's own Heptaplus text (quoted by Wallis) already limits angelic knowledge of God to what is manifest in their own substance, so the later work sharpens rather than reverses this qualification of angelic perfection.

Still's report that Pico calls even angelic intellectual knowledge imperfect, because it reaches outside itself for the light of truth it lacks, restates Pico's own claim in the treatise about the imperfection of angelic knowledge.

Still argues that despite the difference of context there is a discernible consistency between the Oration's ascent and De ente's sobriety about angelic knowledge, qualifying his own prior observation that the later work is 'perhaps more sober'.

judged.justification: Shows De ente et uno treating angelic knowledge as itself imperfect, which qualifies the Oration's ladder.

quotes.t: it comes as no surprise that his last completed work, De ente et uno, closes with a similar message that exhorts readers to unify cognition and life toward God: “If these three, one, true, and good, follow by perpetual connection, …

The intention, however, is unmistakable, for it maintains that humans should realize the convergence of the transcendentals (being, one, true, good) – that is, the principles of cognition and the highest attributes of God – in their life by way …

rel.basis: Dougherty's quotation of Pico's closing lines, that when we are not one, true and good we absolutely are not, is Pico's own text word for word.

Dougherty's reading that the treatise exhorts realizing the convergence of the transcendentals in life by returning to God is borne out by Pico's own claim that unless sense is bound to reason by virtue we are a kingdom divided against itself.

a dispute between the Platonists – in the persons of Lorenzo de’ Medici and Marsilio Ficino – and the Peripatetics or those who, like Poliziano, had always studied the texts of Aristotle. In reality, Pico seemed to disagree with the …

rel.basis: Borghesi says Poliziano asked Pico to intervene between the Platonists in the persons of Lorenzo and Ficino and the Peripatetics; Edelheit has the discussion between Lorenzo and Poliziano only, with Ficino not named as a disputant.
Miller has only Lorenzo maintaining the Platonic view, Ficino merely the source of the tradition Lorenzo followed; Borghesi makes Ficino himself a party to the dispute that occasioned the treatise.

Pico's own words that those who hold Aristotle disagrees with Plato disagree with him, who makes a concordant philosophy of both, bear out Borghesi's claim that Pico used the occasion to state his theories of concord.

The De ente proem records that Lorenzo, 'supported by the reasons of the Platonists', disputed against Aristotle; Borghesi's account, that the work was occasioned by 'a dispute between the Platonists -- in the persons of Lorenzo de' Medici and Marsilio Ficino -- and the Peripatetics', supplies the name the proem itself withholds.

judged.justification: Explains De ente et uno as an intervention in a Florentine dispute between Platonists and Peripatetics, with Pico rejecting the terms of the dispute.
